THE FORGOTTEN CUSTOMER / PRODUCT STRATEGY

The customer didn’t
lose the work.
The product lost the thread.

Aryan had a project in progress. Seven weeks later, the only thing the product remembered was that he was gone.

THE PERSON BEHIND THE SIGNAL / 02
Meet Aryan

He didn’t abandon the goal. He lost momentum.

Aryan used the product every week. He had started a project, saved his progress, and expected to finish it.

BeforeRegularly used the product and saved his work.
ThenWork got busy. A few unfinished steps became harder to face. Returning began to feel like starting over.
NowSeven weeks later, the project is still saved. The context around it is not.

Aryan is a fictional persona. His behaviour and motivations are illustrative hypotheses, not research findings.

THE AUTOMATED RESPONSE / 03

Seven weeks of silence. One message that forgets everything before it.

Aryan gets a win-back offer. It asks him to return, but gives him no reason to.

INBOX · TODAY9:14 AM
PROMOTION

We miss you, Aryan!

It’s been a while. Come back today and enjoy 15% off your next month.

READ THE BEHAVIOUR, NOT THE MIND / 04

His behaviour told a story.
But not the whole story.

These events show the sequence: Aryan opened the project, continued working, encountered a pause, then stopped returning. They locate the drop-off; they do not establish its cause.

A better interpretation

“He didn’t necessarily lose interest. He may simply have lost his place.”

This is a hypothesis inferred from behaviour, not a fact about Aryan’s feelings. The product should respond proportionately to its confidence.

THE EXPERIENCE GAP / 05

A discount can bring him back.
Can the product help him continue?

One plausible barrier is the effort of restarting: locating the project, remembering the decisions already made, and identifying the next unfinished task.

Same customer. Two very different experiences.
THE USUAL WIN-BACK

“Come back for 15% off.”

A reason to open the app. No help with what he left unfinished.

The customer still has to start over.
A MORE RELEVANT RETURN

“Your project is saved. Pick up where you paused.”

The work is waiting. The next step is clear. No need to start again.

Make coming back feel easy.
THE PRODUCT MECHANISM / 06

Turn customer context
into a better next action.

RecallShow the last project opened, the work saved and the most recent completed step.
→
InterpretSeparate observed facts (unfinished setup, unresolved error) from possible explanations (lack of time, changed priorities). Label uncertainty.
→
DecideIf work is saved, link to it. If an error blocked progress, offer help. If the reason is unknown, avoid inventing one.
→
LearnDid the customer complete the next useful task?
High confidenceKnown unfinished task → restore progress.
Medium confidencePossible friction → offer a choice.
Low confidenceUnclear reason → ask gently or wait.
No current needRespect the silence. Don’t manufacture urgency.
The guardrail

Remember what the customer did. Don’t assume you know why.

A BETTER WAY BACK / 07

Don’t send him back to the homepage.
Return him to his progress.

Aryan opens the message and lands straight in his saved project. He can see what’s done — and exactly what’s left.

No hunting through menus. No repeating setup. Just a clear way to carry on.

DESIGN FOR THE REASON, NOT THE SEGMENT / 08

A pause in activity is not a diagnosis.

A stalled setup, a busy week, and a completed goal should not trigger the same message. Select a situation to see how the product should respond.

Product response

Remove the point of friction

Restore saved progress and make the next step obvious. Don’t ask the customer to repeat work they have already done.

What the customer hears
“Your setup is saved. Finish the last two steps whenever you’re ready.”

Send this only when the saved project and unfinished step are confirmed. Make the message easy to dismiss, and stop reminders when the customer opts out or completes the task.

PROVE THE VALUE / 09

Reactivation is not the outcome.
Recovered value is.

Do not count an app open as success. Measure whether the customer completed the unfinished setup, resumed the project, used the product again for its intended job, or renewed when renewal was due.

ReactivationDid dormant customers return?
Meaningful useDid they complete a valuable action?
Incremental valueDid the experience outperform a holdout?

An opened email is not recovery. Track completed tasks, repeat use, retained revenue and opt-outs—and compare them with a holdout group to estimate what the intervention changed.

Validate with a controlled holdout. Track incremental reactivation, repeat use or purchase, retained revenue, and opt-outs. Do not attribute all returning activity to the intervention.
